claims.claim: Duke's regulated grid, generation and storage build links rising electricity demand to transmission/distribution capacity, dispatchable generation and storage; the human need served is reliable, affordable electricity while large-load growth is conditioned on engineering studies and customer protections.

Battery deployment and a diversified nuclear/gas/renewables/storage mix reduce dependence on any single generation technology, but regulatory approval, financing cost and realized load growth remain successor bottlenecks.

causalEdges: large-load/economic growth -> electricity demand -> grid/generation/storage investment -> regulated service capacity -> reliability/affordability
generation intermittency/peak demand -> storage -> dispatch flexibility -> reliability
regulatory approval + financing cost + realized load growth -> capital recovery -> investment durability

risks.risk: If forecast large-load growth fails to materialize, excess capacity or stranded-cost pressure can weaken the causal investment case.

unknowns.unknown: Independent regulator evidence on realized customer savings from the large-load framework remains outside this Beta pass.

claims.claim: The strongest present falsifiers are financing/dilution, regulatory recovery and load-forecast error rather than a demonstrated operating contradiction: Duke priced $1.75B of equity units in August 2026 while pursuing a capital-intensive modernization program.
Customer-protection terms for large loads reduce but do not eliminate stranded-asset and affordability risk if demand forecasts or regulatory assumptions fail.

risks.risk: Equity-linked financing evidences real capital intensity and potential dilution exposure.
Regulated returns depend on timely approvals and cost recovery; forecast error can shift pressure toward customers or shareholders.

unknowns.unknown: This pass does not quantify fully diluted share impact from the equity units or jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction allowed-return sensitivity.
